chapter_theme: The greatness of the Agamas (ஆகமச் சிறப்பு): the Lord gave the Siva Agamas by grace, through a chain from Siva to Nandi; they are past counting, yet without the knowledge the Lord declared they are writing on water. He spoke them in Sanskrit and Tamil alike, and both languages make him known.
structure_note: The Agamas' origin and number (57, 58, 60), their transmission and names (61 to 63), the warning that their number is worthless without knowledge (64), and the two languages of revelation (59, 65, 66).

57.reading: The twenty-eight Agamas are the rare meaning that the sixty-six, with joined palms, heard from the fearless face of the one who has the dark-bodied woman as half of himself.
57.nuance: அஞ்சொடு இருபத்துமூன்று (five with twenty-three) gives the traditional count of 28 Saiva Agamas. அஞ்சா முகம் may be 'fearless face' or, punning, அஞ்சு ஆம் முகம், the five faces from which tradition says the Agamas came. Who the sixty-six hearers are the verse does not say.

58.reading: The Siva Agamas the Lord gives by his grace number twenty-eight crore hundred-thousand; they told the greatness of the Lord of the gods, and I, keeping that meaning in mind, praise it.
58.nuance: The number is a figure of vastness, not a count. The verse turns at the end to the poet's own task: what he praises is the meaning (அப்பொருள்), not the bulk.

59.reading: Say that the learned are those who know the intent of what the seers of the eighteen languages say; the eighteen languages of the learned are the way the First of the cosmos told dharma.
59.nuance: பதினெட்டுப் பாடை is usually taken as the eighteen languages of the land. On that reading the verse makes every language a channel of the Lord's dharma and the learned those who grasp intent rather than words. Whether பதினெட்டும் pairs with பாடையும் or names eighteen other things is unclear.

60.reading: The divine Agamas the Lord gives by his grace are hard to understand even for the immortals in heaven; counted, they come to seventy crore hundred-thousand, and even that count is writing on water.
60.nuance: The last line can mean that the number itself is meaningless, or, as 64 states outright, that the Agamas are writing on water for anyone who does not understand them. The number differs from 58 (twenty-eight crore), which suggests both are figures of vastness.

61.reading: When the Supreme, showing the supreme-beyond, as support of the world, himself spoke the Siva dharma, Nandi, worshipped by the immortals as Hara, became its strength and stood high as the Agama.
61.nuance: பரம் and பராபரம் are technical terms for the Supreme and what lies beyond it. தரனாய், அரனாய், உரனாகி rhyme and are hard to separate: Nandi may be Siva himself here, or the first receiver who becomes the Agama's support.

62.reading: The nine Agamas that, from Siva as the Supreme, Shakti, Sadasiva, Mahesa, the Rudra gods, Vishnu, Brahma and the Lord received each from the other, our Nandi received.
62.nuance: The verse gives a chain of transmission ending in Nandi, Tirumular's own teacher. உவமா and தவமால் பிரமீசர் may divide in other ways, so the exact list of links is not certain. The nine Agamas are named in 63.

63.reading: The good Agamas he received are Karanam, Kamikam, the noble Viram, the lofty Sinthiyam, Vathulam, Yamalam, Kalottaram, the good Suppiram and Makutam.
63.nuance: These are names from the traditional list of 28 Agamas (Karana, Kamika, Vira, Cintya, Vatula, Yamala, Kalottara, Suprabheda and Makuta). சுப்பிரம் is taken as Suprabheda.

64.reading: Though the Siva Agamas the Lord gives by his grace are gathered in countless crores, if one does not know the knowledge the Lord declared, all those crores are writing on water.
64.nuance: The verse repeats 58's first line and turns it against bulk: the measure of the Agamas is the knowledge (அறிவு) they carry, not their number. அண்ணல் அறைந்த அறிவு may be the Lord's teaching or the knowledge of the Lord.

65.reading: Standing while rain and summer and long dew pass, while even the lake wanes, he spoke Sanskrit and Tamil together and showed grace to the lady.
65.nuance: காரிகையார் (the lady) is traditionally the Goddess, to whom Siva is said to have taught the Agamas. The first two lines may describe his standing through the seasons, or her long penance before he taught her. ஆரியம் here means Sanskrit, and the verse names it and Tamil as given together.

66.reading: How the soul is loosed, how it is bound, and how life departs in the blink of an eye: the Tamil word and the northern word, these two, teach him, and through them one can come to know him.
66.nuance: அவிழ்கின்ற, கட்டும் (loosing, binding) are read as release and bondage; the verse does not name the soul. The plain claim is that Tamil and Sanskrit equally lead to knowing the Lord.

links.note: Both end in நீர்மேல் எழுத்து, writing on water. 60 leaves open what is futile; 64 states the condition: Agamas without the knowledge the Lord declared.

The Kural asks what learning is worth if one does not bow at the feet of the one of pure knowledge; Tirumular says crores of Agamas are writing on water without the knowledge the Lord declared. Both measure scripture by what it leads to.

The Naladiyar says worldly books without the books of wisdom are only clamour that never removes confusion; Tirumular says even the Agamas, if their knowledge is missed, are writing on water. Both deny that bulk of learning is the point.

Both face writing beyond counting. The Naladiyar's answer is to choose what is fitting, like the bird that drinks the milk and leaves the water; Tirumular's is that the countless Agamas are hard even for the gods and their count is writing on water.
65 says the Lord spoke Sanskrit and Tamil together; 66 says what both teach, bondage, release and death, and that either leads to knowing him.
59 widens the languages of the Lord's dharma to eighteen; 66 names two, Tamil and Sanskrit. Both refuse to tie revelation to one tongue.

58 gives the Siva Agamas a vast count (இருபத்தெண் கோடிநூறாயிரம்) and says the poet praises their meaning. 64 repeats 58's first line word for word and then turns it: if the knowledge the Lord declared (அண்ணல் அறைந்த அறிவு) is not known, countless crores are writing on water. The pair shows the book setting up the Agamas' bulk and then making its worth conditional on understanding.

59 says the learned are those who know the intent (கருத்தறிவார்) of what the seers of the eighteen languages say, whatever the language. Kural 423 says wisdom is seeing the true thing (மெய்ப்பொருள் காண்பது) in whatever is heard, from whoever's mouth (யார்யார்வாய்க் கேட்பினும்). Both place learning in grasping meaning regardless of the source's tongue or speaker.

61 says the Supreme himself spoke the Siva dharma and Nandi stood as the Agama (ஆகமம் ஓங்கிநின்றானே). 2397 says the Veda and the Agama are the true Lord's scripture (மெய்யாம் இறைவன்நூல்) and both are his word (நாதன் உரையவை). The late verse states as doctrine what the preface tells as a scene of origin: scripture is the Lord's own speech.

62 traces the nine Agamas down a chain from Siva through Shakti, Sadasiva and the gods until 'our Nandi received' them (நந்திபெற்றானே). 67 takes the chain on from Nandi: the masters who received Nandi's grace (நந்தி அருள்பெற்ற நாதர்) are eight, Tirumular among them. Read together, the two chapters give one unbroken line of transmission from Siva to the poet.
